quick_notes.title: Divisibility Rules
quick_notes.detail: 2 (Even), 3 (Sum of digits divisible by 3), 4 (Last 2 digits), 5 (Ends in 0/5), 8 (Last 3 digits), 9 (Sum of digits divisible by 9), 11 (Diff of sum of odd and even places is 0 or multiple of 11).
quick_notes.explanation: Divisibility rules are shortcuts to check if one number can be evenly divided by another without doing long division. A number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is an even number, like 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. For 3, add up all the digits of the number, and if that total can be divided by 3 with no remainder, then the original number is divisible by 3. To check 4, look only at the last two digits of the number; if those two digits form a number that is divisible by 4, then the whole number is. For 5, the number must end in either 0 or 5. For 8, look at the last three digits; if that three-digit number is divisible by 8, then the whole number is. For 9, add up all the digits, and if that sum is divisible by 9, the original number is. Finally, for 11, add the digits in the odd positions (first, third, fifth, and so on) and separately add the digits in the even positions (second, fourth, sixth); then subtract the even sum from the odd sum, and if the result is 0 or a multiple of 11 (like 11, 22, 33), the original number is divisible by 11.

quick_notes.title: Unit Digit Trick
quick_notes.detail: Cyclicity of digits. 2, 3, 7, 8 have cyclicity of 4. 0, 1, 5, 6 remain same. 4 and 9 have cyclicity of 2.
quick_notes.explanation: The unit digit is the last digit of a number. Cyclicity means the repeating pattern of unit digits when you raise a base number to different powers. The digits 2, 3, 7, and 8 each repeat their unit digit after every 4 powers, so they have a cyclicity of 4. The digits 0, 1, 5, and 6 always give the same unit digit no matter what power you use. The digits 4 and 9 repeat every 2 powers,

quick_notes.title: Remainder Theorem
quick_notes.detail: If a polynomial f(x) is divided by (x-a), the remainder is f(a). Positive and Negative remainders concept is useful for large powers.
quick_notes.explanation: The Remainder Theorem is a shortcut for finding the remainder when you divide a polynomial by a simple expression like (x minus a). A polynomial is a math expression with variables and powers, like x squared plus 3x plus 2. The theorem says that if you divide a polynomial, which we call f(x), by (x minus a), the remainder you get is exactly the same as plugging the number a into the polynomial, written as f(a). For example, if you divide x squared plus 3x plus 2 by (x minus 1), the remainder is f(1), which means you replace every x with 1, so 1 squared plus 3 times 1 plus 2 equals 1 plus 3 plus 2, which is 6. This is useful for large powers because you can sometimes use the idea of positive and negative remainders to find the remainder without doing all the long division.

quick_notes.title: HCF & LCM
quick_notes.detail: HCF (Highest Common Factor). LCM (Lowest Common Multiple). Property : Product of two numbers : HCF × LCM.
quick_notes.explanation: HCF stands for Highest Common Factor, which is the largest number that divides two or more numbers exactly, with no remainder. LCM stands for Lowest Common Multiple, which is the smallest number that is a multiple of two or more numbers. A key property connecting these two is that for any two numbers, the product of the numbers is always equal to the product of their HCF and LCM. For example, if the numbers are 6 and 8, their product is 48, and the HCF is 2 while the LCM is 24, and 2 multiplied by 24 gives 48. This means if you know any two of these three values, you can always find the third one by multiplying or dividing.

quick_notes.title: Number of Zeros
quick_notes.detail: Number of zeros at the end of n! is determined by the number of pairs of 2 and 5. Since 5s are fewer, count the powers of 5.
quick_notes.explanation: To find how many zeros are at the end of n! (which is n factorial, meaning the product of all whole numbers from 1 up to n, for example 5! equals 1 times 2 times 3 times 4 times 5 which is 120), you need to count the number of times the number 10 can be made as a factor. Since 10 equals 2 times 5, and in any factorial there are always more factors of 2 than factors of 5, the number of zeros is determined by the total number of factors of 5 in the product. To get this total, you divide n by 5, then divide the result by 5 again, and keep dividing by 5 until you get a number smaller than 5, then add up all those quotients. For example, to find the zeros at the end of 25!, you first divide 25 by 5 to get 5, then divide 5 by 5 to get 1, and since 1 is less than 5 you stop, and adding 5 plus 1 gives 6 zeros at the end of 25!.
